l: Midas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: Midas, king of the Phrygian people, hospitably receives Silenus and restores him to Bacchus. He receives the power to turn whatever he touches into gold, but the power leaves him rich and wretched when it transforms his food and drink; after repenting, he bathes at the source of the Pactolus and is freed from it.

l: Orpheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: Orpheus is identified as the victim of the Thracian women's murder, for which Bacchus punishes them. He had entrusted the mysterious orgies of Bacchus to Midas and the Cecropian Eumolpus.

l: Pactolus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: The Pactolus is the river adjoining great Sardis to which Bacchus sends Midas. When Midas plunges into its bubbling source, the golden power leaves his body and enters the stream.

l: gold, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: Under Midas's touch, twigs, stones, clods, wheat, apples, door-posts, water, food, and drink become gold. The gold that enters the Pactolus remains associated with the river's sands and the surrounding fields.

l: Midas's golden-touch power, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: Bacchus grants Midas's request that everything he touches with his body turn into gold. The power proves harmful because it makes food and drink inedible, and Bacchus later annuls it when Midas repents.

l: Midas's purification in the Pactolus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: Bacchus instructs Midas to follow the Pactolus upstream to its source and plunge his head beneath the bubbling spring. Midas obeys, and the golden virtue leaves his body and passes into the river.

l: Midas's request for the golden touch, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: Midas asks Bacchus to make everything he touches with his body turn into yellow gold. Bacchus grants the request but regrets that Midas did not ask for something better.

l: Midas's repentance, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: After discovering that his food and drink have become gold, Midas recognizes that he has done wrong and begs Bacchus to deliver him from the calamity. Bacchus accepts his confession, restores him to his former state, and directs him to the Pactolus.

l: golden sands of the Pactolus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE II. [XI.85-145]
s: The Pactolus acquires its golden sands when Midas's golden power passes from his body into the river. The surrounding fields are thereafter described as bearing gold from the ancient vein.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Pan challenges Apollo to a musical contest before the mountain god Tmolus, with Nymphs and Midas present. Tmolus judges Apollo's lyre music superior to Pan's rustic reeds, and everyone agrees except Midas. Apollo punishes Midas by giving him ass's ears, which Midas hides beneath a purple turban. Midas's barber discovers the ears and secretly tells the earth, from which a grove of reeds later reveals the secret.

l: Pan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Pan boasts of his reed music to the Nymphs and challenges Apollo, daring to consider his playing superior. He loses the contest when Tmolus judges Apollo's music better.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Apollo competes with Pan and plays his lyre with the skill and posture of an artist. His music charms Tmolus, who judges it superior to Pan's.

l: Tmolus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Tmolus serves as umpire of the contest between Pan and Apollo. After hearing both performances, he favors Apollo, and his judgment pleases everyone except Midas.

l: Midas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Midas is present during the musical contest and foolishly prefers Pan's music to Apollo's. Apollo punishes him by changing his human ears into the ears of an ass, which Midas conceals beneath a purple turban.

l: Midas's barber, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Midas's barber discovers the ass's ears while cutting Midas's hair. Unable either to reveal the secret openly or keep it to himself, he whispers it into a hole in the ground and covers it again.

l: Pan's rustic music, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Pan's rustic music is produced by reeds joined with wax. Tmolus hears it but finds Apollo's lyre music superior, and Midas is the only one who praises it above Apollo's.

l: Apollo's lyre music, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Apollo's lyre music is played with a plectrum and a skilful thumb. Its sweetness charms Tmolus and leads him to judge Apollo's performance better than Pan's.

l: contest between Pan and Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: The contest takes place under Tmolus's arbitration while Nymphs and Midas are present. Apollo wins the unequal contest, although Midas alone calls the decision unjust.

l: judgment of Tmolus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Tmolus's judgment favors Apollo's lyre over Pan's reeds. The whole company approves the decision except Midas, whose contrary opinion results in his punishment.

l: ass's ears (Midas), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV, FABLE III. [XI.146-193]
s: Apollo gives Midas ears that are long, covered with grey hairs, unsteady at the lower part, and capable of movement. Midas hides them under a purple turban, but the secret is eventually revealed by reeds growing from the place where his barber whispered it.
